claims.subject: rama
claims.summary: Agastya gives Rama a divine bow, inexhaustible quivers and a sword, describing them as weapons once used by Viṣṇu.
claims.speaker: Agastya
claims.note: A narrated gift at their meeting; introductory commentary on the page is excluded.

claims.subject: lakshmana
claims.summary: Lakṣmaṇa introduces himself to Agastya’s disciple as Rama’s younger brother and says the brothers entered the forest at their father’s order.
claims.speaker: Lakṣmaṇa
claims.note: Reported speech to the disciple, before the meeting with Agastya.

claims.subject: rama
claims.summary: Lakṣmaṇa identifies Rama as Daśaratha’s eldest son when requesting an audience with Agastya.
claims.speaker: Lakṣmaṇa
claims.note: The relationship is stated in an audience request, not as a separate chronology date.

claims.subject: sita
claims.summary: Lakṣmaṇa identifies Sītā as Rama’s wife while announcing their arrival at Agastya’s hermitage.
claims.speaker: Lakṣmaṇa
claims.note: Directly stated in reported speech to the disciple.

claims.subject: sutikshna
claims.summary: After spending time with Sutīkṣṇa, Rama takes leave and proceeds to visit Agastya; the account places this visit after the narrated ten-year period among nearby hermitages.
claims.note: The ten years belong to Rama’s itinerary in this narrative, not to Agastya’s age.

claims.subject: epic_pitrs
claims.summary: Agastya’s suspended ancestors tell him that they remain in that state for want of his offspring and ask him to beget a son.
claims.speaker: Agastya’s ancestors, in Lomasa’s narration
claims.note: The episode motivates the marriage and progeny narrative; it is a narrated past, not a meeting with Yudhiṣṭhira.

claims.subject: vidarbha_king
claims.summary: The unnamed Vidarbha king is unwilling to give his daughter but fears Agastya’s curse if he refuses.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: The king remains unnamed in this passage; not assigned another identity.

claims.subject: lopamudra
claims.summary: Seeing her parents distressed, Lopāmudrā tells her father to give her to Agastya and spare himself anxiety.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: The daughter’s own consent is explicit in this telling.

claims.subject: lopamudra
claims.summary: After their marriage, Agastya and Lopāmudrā go to Gaṅgādvāra and practice austerities together.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: Narrated after the marriage; this is a narrative sequence, with no absolute date.

claims.subject: lopamudra
claims.summary: Before agreeing to marital intercourse, Lopāmudrā asks Agastya for a bed, adornments and attire like those she had in her father’s palace.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: This request motivates Agastya’s subsequent search for wealth; no modern chronological inference is implied.

claims.subject: srutarvan
claims.summary: After declining to take wealth from Śrutarvan because his income matched his expenses, Agastya takes that king with him to Vṛdhnaśva.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: Narrative sequence among named kings; Ganguli section locator is not a BORI chapter number.

claims.subject: vradhnasva
claims.summary: After Vṛdhnaśva also declines to provide surplus wealth, he joins Agastya and Śrutarvan on the visit to Trasadasyu.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: The passage calls Trasadasyu Purokutsa’s son and places him in Ikṣvāku’s line; this epic witness is not identified with Vedic namesakes.

claims.subject: ilvala
claims.summary: Lomasa says Ilvala transforms his brother Vātāpi into a ram, serves his cooked flesh to Brahmins, then summons him to emerge and kill them.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: Narrated background for the later encounter; it is not a separate meeting between Agastya and the brothers.

claims.subject: mahabharata
claims.summary: At Ilvala’s feast Agastya eats the served Vātāpi and says he has digested him before he can emerge.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: The narrative presents the act as defeating the brothers’ recurring killing stratagem.

claims.subject: ilvala
claims.summary: Ilvala gives Agastya the wealth the sage names, including twice the amount offered to each king, a golden chariot and two horses.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: Agastya states the intended gift; Ilvala checks and then gives it. The named kings also receive wealth.

claims.subject: dridhasyu
claims.summary: Lomasa says the foetus remained in Lopāmudrā’s womb seven years before Dṛḍhasyu was born; as a child he carried sacrificial fuel and was called Idhmavāha.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: The epithet and the seven-year gestation belong to this epic story; they do not independently date Agastya or identify a different Dṛḍhasyu.

claims.subject: epic_pitrs
claims.summary: The narration says Agastya’s ancestors obtain the desired state after he begets Dṛḍhasyu.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: This is the story’s stated consequence of the son’s birth.

claims.subject: mahabharata
claims.summary: Agastya asks Vindhya for a path to the southern region and tells the mountain to wait until his return; the narrator says he has not returned up to the story’s present.
claims.speaker: Lomasa
claims.note: A narrative synchronism only. Ganguli’s section numbers are not BORI chapter numbers; no absolute date follows.

claims.subject: nahusha
claims.summary: In Agastya’s account to Indra, Nahuṣa touches the sage’s head with his foot while the sages carry him; Agastya then curses him to fall from heaven and roam as a serpent for ten thousand years.
claims.speaker: Agastya, in Śalya’s narration
claims.note: This adds the trigger and sequence to the core curse claim. Ten thousand years describes Nahuṣa’s curse, not Agastya’s lifespan.

findings: Rāmāyaṇa 3.12: receives Agastya’s weapons; the meeting occurs after the 3.11 itinerary sequence.
Rāmāyaṇa 3.12: identifies himself as Rama’s younger brother while seeking audience.
Rāmāyaṇa 3.12: identified by Lakṣmaṇa as Rama’s wife; the existing 3.13 claim compares her to Arundhatī.
Rāmāyaṇa 3.12: named by Lakṣmaṇa as Rama’s father.
No new claim; core graph already records the 3.13 comparison with Sītā.
Rāmāyaṇa 3.11 places Rama’s departure from Sutīkṣṇa before the Agastya visit; the narrated ten-year itinerary is Rama’s.
No additional evidence checked; core graph already records Sugrīva’s speech about Agastya in Rāmāyaṇa 4.41.
No additional evidence checked; core graph already records the Ādityahṛdaya instruction in Rāmāyaṇa 6.105 (site numbering).
In Vana Parva §96, Lomasa narrates Agastya’s past to Yudhiṣṭhira; §§97–99 continue that account. This is not an Agastya–Yudhiṣṭhira meeting.
Vana Parva §96: asks Lomasa about Agastya’s slaying of Vātāpi while at Agastya’s former hermitage.
Udyoga Parva §17: narrates to Yudhiṣṭhira Agastya’s account to Indra after Nahuṣa’s fall.
Udyoga Parva §17 supplies the kick as the trigger of Agastya’s curse and gives Nahuṣa’s serpent-term; it is not an Agastya lifespan.
Vana Parva §98: accompanies Agastya after the sage declines to take wealth from him, then goes with him to Vṛdhnaśva.
Vana Parva §98: joins Agastya and Śrutarvan on the next visit, to Trasadasyu.
Vana Parva §98 calls this Trasadasyu Purokutsa’s son and places him in Ikṣvāku’s line; identity with Vedic attestations remains unestablished here.
open_questions: Compare epic and Vedic occurrences only with source-specific evidence; do not merge on name alone.

findings: Vana Parva §§96, 99: Ilvala uses Vātāpi as a food-based killing stratagem; Agastya defeats it and Ilvala gives wealth.
Vana Parva §§96, 99: named as Ilvala’s younger brother, transformed into a ram, and digested by Agastya.
Vana Parva §97: the unnamed king fears refusing Agastya; Lopāmudrā herself asks him to consent.
open_questions: King’s personal name is not supplied in this passage.

findings: Vana Parva §99: Dṛḍhasyu is born after seven years in the womb and is also called Idhmavāha for carrying fuel.
open_questions: Keep separate from other figures with the same or similar name unless independently identified.

findings: No new epic claim. The Bhāgavata witness remains the person in the core graph; no same-name epic figure is merged with him.
